**Welcome to STAT 312!** Engineers and scientists routinely work with data that contain variability and uncertainty. For example, how can we determine whether a change in a manufacturing process actually improves product quality? How can we use measurements from a sample to draw conclusions about a larger population? How can we quantify uncertainty when comparing two designs, estimating an unknown quantity, or predicting future performance?

**Statistics and probability** provide a framework for answering these questions. They allow us to collect and summarize data, understand variability, quantify uncertainty, draw meaningful conclusions, and make informed decisions.

Throughout the semester, we will develop the fundamental statistical and probabilistic tools used in **engineering and scientific problem solving**. Topics will include descriptive statistics, probability and probability distributions, sampling distributions, estimation, confidence intervals, hypothesis testing, and regression analysis. Our emphasis will be on developing statistical reasoning and intuition, understanding when and why particular methods are appropriate, and applying those methods to real-world problems. Rather than simply memorizing formulas, you will learn to select appropriate statistical methods, carry out analyses, interpret results, evaluate assumptions, and communicate conclusions in the context of the problem being studied.

# Learning Objectives


Upon completion of this course, students should be able to:

- Build, use, and interpret **graphical and numerical summaries** of data.

- Apply fundamental concepts of **probability**, including conditional probability, independence, random variables, and probability distributions, to engineering and scientific problems.

- Identify and work with commonly used **discrete and continuous probability distributions**, and recognize situations in which they provide appropriate models.

- Understand **sampling variability and sampling distributions**, including the role of the Central Limit Theorem in statistical inference.

- Use sample data to **estimate unknown population parameters** and quantify uncertainty using standard errors and confidence intervals.

- Formulate appropriate **statistical hypotheses**, conduct hypothesis tests, interpret p-values, and draw conclusions in the context of an engineering or scientific problem.

- Build, interpret, and evaluate **simple linear regression and correlation models**, and use regression models for estimation and prediction.

- Use appropriate **statistical tools and software**, when needed, to support statistical calculations, data analysis, and interpretation.

- **Interpret and communicate statistical results** clearly using appropriate terminology, notation, reasoning, and evidence.

## Statistical software

We will use the (completely free and open source) R programming language for some data analysis in this course. RStudio (an interface for R) facilitates the use of R. 

- Desktop version: Download for Windows or Mac at <https://posit.co/downloads/>. Note: You first need to download and install R on your computer in order to use the desktop version of RStudio

- Library: Resources offered by Kelvin Smith Library are available [here](https://researchguides.case.edu/randrstudio)

More detailed instructions on downloading, installing, and getting started with R, and RStudio are available on the [R Resources](R_Resources.qmd) tab.

# The 5 Core Components 

## (1) Engagement

Engagement is important to your own learning & to fostering a supportive learning community.

::: {.callout-important title="📌 Expectations"}
- **Do not miss in-person class sessions (except emergency situation).** 
- **When attending class:**
  - Be on time & don’t leave early  
  - Do not use your phone (phones must be put away when you enter the course, even if class hasn’t started)  
  - [Do not use your laptop for anything other than taking notes and in-class activities](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0360131512002254) (e.g., no videos, no email, no messaging apps, etc.)  
  - Be actively present (e.g., don’t work alone, don’t work on other courses, etc.)  

- **Outside class:**
  - Check your email for canvas announcements and stay updated on the Canvas Discussion forum  
  - When you have questions, or just want to chat, please stop by OH!
  
:::


## (2) Practice Problems (PP) {-}

Complete the **Practice Problems (PP)** before attempting the HW assignments. Working through the PP alongside the lecture notes and class materials will deepen your understanding of the core concepts and help you feel more confident when tackling homework problems. Consistent practice will also make your exam preparation easier and more effective.

There are two types of Practice Problems:

### Required Practice Problems {-}

Complete the **Required Practice Problems** throughout the unit as we cover the corresponding topics in class.

These problems reinforce the concepts discussed in the lecture notes, handouts, and other course resources.

Before attempting the HW assignments and preparing for exams, make sure you have completed and reviewed all Required Practice Problems from the unit.

### Supplemental Practice Problems {-}

The **Supplemental Practice Problems** provide additional practice opportunities for students who would like more practice with the concepts covered in the unit.

Complete the Required Practice Problems first, and then use the Supplemental Practice Problems as needed for additional review and practice.


## (3) Quizzes

Each quiz assesses your general understanding of the topics covered during the corresponding unit. Detailed directions and policies are here: [STAT 312 HW Assignment & Quiz policies](https://docs.google.com/document/d/10uit5Ei_a8cuqM8pVsNkqBOny6KRLkjTkLocBhI7nFA/edit?usp=sharing).


## (3) HW Assignments

In the HW assignments, you will practice and explore the course material in more depth. Detailed directions and policies are here: [STAT 312 HW Assignment & Quiz policies](https://docs.google.com/document/d/10uit5Ei_a8cuqM8pVsNkqBOny6KRLkjTkLocBhI7nFA/edit?usp=sharing).



## (4) Exams (Content Expertise)

Your course engagement, collaboration, preparation, practice, and application will support your deeper understanding of the course material. This will be assessed through three in-person exams. You must schedule all travel and other commitments around them - there will not be any alternative exam times.

- **Midterm Exam 1:** Monday, Oct 5 (Tentative Date)
- **Midterm Exam 2:** Monday, Nov 9 (Tentative Date)
- **Final Exam (Comprehensive):** *Finals week*  
  - The final exam will be written to take ~1.25 hours, but you will have the full 2-hour period to complete it.  
    - 10:25–11:15am section 103: Dec 14, 8:00-10:00am in class
    - 11:30am–12:20pm section 104: Dec 9, 8:00-10:00am in class
    - 2:05–2:55pm section 105: Dec 16, 12:00-2:00pm in class


::: {.callout-warning title="📜 Exam Policies"}
- **All Exams will have the following format:**
  - Taken individually, using pen/pencil & paper  
  - You may use a physical calculator (not the calculator in your phone) in the exam
  - Closed notes, but you may use one sheet of paper, with writing on one side (two sided writing is NOT permitted) for the midterm exams. These can be handwritten or typed, but you cannot include screenshots or share formula sheet. Making your own Formula Sheet is important to the review process - as you are required to submit the Formula Sheet along with the answer paper.
- **Final Exam will be comprehensive.** For the final exam, you may use one sheet of paper, with writing in both sides.

:::

**Title IX:** You deserve a community free from discrimination, sexual harassment, hostility, sexual assault, domestic violence, dating violence, and stalking. If you or anyone you know has experienced harassment or discrimination, know that you are not alone. CWRU provides staff and resources to help you find support. **Please be aware that as a faculty member, it is my responsibility to report disclosure about sexual harassment, sexual misconduct, relationship violence, and stalking to the Title IX Office.** The purpose of this report is to ensure that anyone experiencing harm receives the resources and support they need. I will keep this information private, and it will not be shared beyond this required report.

You may also contact CWRU’s Title IX Coordinator directly (phone: 216-368-3066; e-mail: rachel.lutner\@case.edu); they will provide you with supportive measures, resources, and referrals. Additional information about how to file a report (including anonymously) is available on the [Title IX website](https://case.edu/equity/title-ix-sex-discrimination-and-sex-based-harassment).

**General Health and Well-being:** I care that you prioritize your well-being in this semester and beyond. Investing time into taking care of yourself will have profound impacts on all aspects of your life. Remember that beyond being a student, you are a human being carrying your own experiences, thoughts, emotions, and identities. It is important to acknowledge any stressors you may be facing, which can be mental, emotional, physical, cultural, financial, etc., and how they can have an impact on you. I encourage you to remember that you have a body with needs. In the classroom, eat when you are hungry, drink water, use the restroom, and step out if you are upset and need some air. Please do what is necessary so long as it does not impede your or others' ability to be mentally and emotionally present in the course. Outside of the classroom, sleeping well, moving your body, and connecting with others can be strategies can help nourish you. If you are having difficulties maintaining your well-being, please don't hesitate to contact me and/or find support from physical and mental health resources [here](https://case.edu/wellness/campuswide-resources/mental-health-resources)and [here](https://case.edu/studentlife/graduate/resources/wellness/physical-wellness-facilities).
